2-5.title: Visit a tobacco cessation clinic or call the National Tobacco Quitline on 1800-11-2356
2-5.cost: A clinic visit is free or nearly so in a government hospital and costs more in a private one. Behavioural support usually means 4–8 sessions of 30–60 minutes. The quitline call is free.
2-5.inPlainWords: Medications and regular follow-up support from professionals are two distinct components that work best together. People who take medication while receiving dedicated follow-up have nearly twice the quit rate of those who only receive brief advice. Phone support also helps: those who proactively call the smoking cessation helpline see their success rate rise by 20–30% compared to others.
2-5.benefit: Across 52 trials involving 19,488 participants, the combination of medication and behavioral support led to a 1.83-fold higher quit rate than standard care or brief advice (RR 1.83, 95% CI 1.68–1.98; high-quality evidence). For the 43 trials conducted in medical settings, this advantage rose to 1.97-fold (95% CI 1.79–2.18). When looking at phone-based support alone: among people who called the helpline themselves, those receiving multiple follow-up calls had a 38% higher quit rate than those who only got informational materials or a single consultation (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.19–1.61; 14 trials, 32,484 participants). For people who did not call the helpline but received scheduled phone support from researchers, the success rate was 25% higher than those without such support (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.15–1.35; 65 trials, 41,233 participants). Both findings are supported by evidence of moderate certainty.
2-5.sources: Stead LF, Koilpillai P, Fanshawe TR, Lancaster T (2016). Combined pharmacotherapy and behavioural interventions for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 3, CD008286. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD008286.pub3>; Matkin W, Ordóñez-Mena JM, Hartmann-Boyce J (2019). Telephone counselling for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 5, CD002850. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD002850.pub4>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>; National Tobacco Control Programme. <https://ntcp.mohfw.gov.in/>
2-5.caveats: In India, ask for a tobacco cessation clinic at a district hospital or medical college under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke, or call the National Tobacco Quitline on 1800-11-2356. Most of the trials above were conducted overseas, and the intensity of local services varies, so treat the figures as general guidance. The medicines are listed in Section 3 of this chapter.

2-40.title: Buy packaged cooking oil that carries an FSSAI licence number; be wary of loose, unlabelled ghani oil of unknown origin
2-40.cost: The price difference is modest if you buy branded packaged oil from a shop; a litre of mustard or groundnut oil costs what it costs, and the packaging is part of the price. What it takes is reading the label: the pack must show an FSSAI licence or registration number, a batch number and a best-before date. The real difficulty is persuading older family members who swear by the oil pressed at a local ghani.
2-40.inPlainWords: When peanuts and oilseed go damp and mouldy they produce aflatoxin, a confirmed human carcinogen that damages the liver, and cold-pressing does not remove it. Loose oil sold from a drum or from a shop’s own press, with no label and no licence number, is where the risk sits: it escapes the routine sampling that packaged oil goes through. Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, anyone manufacturing, processing, packing or selling cooking oil must hold an FSSAI licence or registration, and packaged oil has to meet the contaminant limits in the FSS (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Regulations, 2011. A licence number is not a guarantee of purity, but it is what makes the seller traceable and a bad batch recallable.
2-40.benefit: Aflatoxin is a Group 1 carcinogen in the International Agency for Research on Cancer classification, meaning it is established to cause cancer in humans, liver cancer above all. Measurements of home-pressed peanut oil from small producers in Guangzhou between 2010 and 2022 found a median aflatoxin B1 concentration of 1.29 μg/kg, with half of all samples between 0.12 and 6.58 μg/kg. After local rules for small producers took effect, levels fell by 2.865 μg/kg at once and by a further 2.593 μg/kg each year, and the share of local residents with abnormal liver function fell by 35% (PR 0.650, 95% CI 0.469-0.902). A cohort of 1,611 pregnant women found that 81.7% ate home-pressed peanut oil, and that those who did had a nearly 90% higher risk of a low-birth-weight baby (adjusted OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.1-3.2) and an 80% higher risk of preterm delivery (adjusted OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1-3.0). These are studies of small oil-pressers elsewhere; they are cited because the product, the mould and the toxin are the same wherever oil is pressed without testing, and published Indian data on aflatoxin in ghani oil is thin.
2-40.sources: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Lei J, Li Y, Wang Y, et al. (2024). The impact of small food workshops management regulations on aflatoxin B1 in home-made peanut oil and the liver function of high-consumption area residents: an interrupted time series study. Frontiers in Public Health, 12. <https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1484414>; Zhong Y, Lu H, Jiang Y, et al. (2024). Effect of homemade peanut oil consumption during pregnancy on low birth weight and preterm birth outcomes: a cohort study. Global Health Action, 17. <https://doi.org/10.1080/16549716.2024.2336312>; International Agency for Research on Cancer (2012). Chemical Agents and Related Occupations. IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, Vol 100F. <https://publications.iarc.fr/123>
2-40.caveats: Both studies are observational, with no randomised control group. The first tracked liver function test results, not liver cancer or deaths. The median aflatoxin level in the home-pressed oil was below the 20 μg/kg limit that Guangzhou food-safety regulators applied at the time (GB 2761-2017, a standard that is not Indian law), so the risk comes from long-term daily consumption and from occasional batches far above the median - which is exactly why a traceable, tested supply matters more than one good sample. Indian contaminant limits apply to all cooking oil sold, licensed or not; what the licence adds is inspection and the ability to trace a bad batch back to a producer. Buying packaged oil does not make it healthy in quantity: it is still fat, and how much you use matters more than the brand. The people who benefit are you and everyone who eats from the same kitchen.

2-46.title: If peanuts, corn, tree nuts, rice or flour go mouldy, throw out the whole packet rather than picking out the visibly spoiled pieces; spit out a bitter nut at once
2-46.cost: Throwing away a spoiled packet of peanuts, dry fruit or grain costs a few tens to a couple of hundred rupees, more for cashews and pistachios. Store dry goods cool, dry and ventilated, buy smaller packets, and do not stockpile before a festival. The hard part is the reluctance to waste food, strongest in the oldest person in the kitchen.
2-46.inPlainWords: Mouldy peanuts and maize produce aflatoxins, potent chemical carcinogens that cause liver cancer. In a long-term prospective cohort of 18,244 middle-aged men in Shanghai, men with detectable aflatoxin in their urine had about 3.4 times the risk of liver cancer of men without it, and men who also carried hepatitis B had about 59 times the risk of men with neither. Aflatoxins survive boiling, roasting and frying.
2-46.benefit: Aflatoxins are Group 1 human carcinogens in the International Agency for Research on Cancer classification, causing hepatocellular carcinoma. They grow most readily on peanuts, maize and tree nuts, and they are heat-stable: ordinary boiling, baking and frying do not destroy them. A prospective cohort enrolled 18,244 middle-aged men in Shanghai from 1986, collected urine at baseline and followed them for roughly 70,000 person-years, during which 55 liver cancers occurred. Comparing 50 cases with 267 matched controls, men with detectable urinary aflatoxin biomarkers had 3.4 times the odds of liver cancer (relative risk 3.4, 95% CI 1.1-10.0). A positive hepatitis B surface antigen test carried 7.3-fold risk (RR 7.3, 95% CI 2.2-24.4). Men positive for both had 59.4-fold risk (RR 59.4, 95% CI 16.6-212.0) against men negative for both. In earlier multivariable analyses adjusted for hepatitis B, smoking, alcohol and education, aflatoxin exposure still carried a 3.8-fold elevation (95% CI 1.2-12.2). In Qidong, Jiangsu Province, a historically high-incidence liver cancer area, the staple shifted in the 1980s from locally stored maize to rice brought in from the regional market: median serum aflatoxin-albumin adducts fell from 19.3 pg/mg in 1989 to undetectable (<0.5 pg/mg) by 2009, and liver cancer mortality in cohorts born after the shift fell by more than half, before infant hepatitis B vaccination was widespread. The researchers attributed about 65% of the decline to lower dietary aflatoxin exposure, with 83% of the averted deaths among chronic hepatitis B carriers. Global risk models put aflatoxin’s carcinogenic potency roughly 30-fold higher in hepatitis B carriers than in non-carriers.
2-46.caveats: The Shanghai figures measure the association between internal biomarker exposure and liver cancer; no trial randomises households to throw out or keep mouldy food. Baseline urine was collected only once in that cohort. In Qidong, serum adducts became undetectable by 2009 following the dietary shift. The magnitude of benefit is rated Moderate because modern household grain storage is vastly better than the historical rural baseline, so exposure today is lower. Why the whole packet: public health agencies advise that once opened nuts or grain show a musty smell or visible mould, invisible fungal threads and spores have spread through the container, and shaking the packet disperses them further. The US Department of Agriculture’s food safety guidance is to discard peanut butter, legumes, nuts, cooked pasta and bread that show any mould; only firm low-moisture vegetables such as cabbage, capsicum or carrot can be salvaged by cutting at least 2.5 cm around the spot. If you bite a nut that tastes bitter or mouldy, spit it out and rinse your mouth. Hepatitis B carriers face this risk multiplied; if you have never checked your hepatitis B status, see Chapter 1, Rule 14. Avoiding unrefined small-workshop peanut oil is Chapter 2, Rule 40. Unspoiled nuts remain worth eating, as Chapter 2, Rule 22 sets out. The people who benefit are you and everyone who shares the meal.

IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, Vol 100F, 225-248. <https://publications.iarc.fr/123>; Qian GS, Ross RK, Yu MC, et al. (1994). A follow-up study of urinary markers of aflatoxin exposure and liver cancer risk in Shanghai. Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention, 3(1), 3-10. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8118382/>; Ross RK, et al. (1992). Urinary aflatoxin biomarkers and risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Lancet, 339(8799), 943-946. <https://doi.org/10.1016/0140-6736(92)91528-G>; Chen JG, Egner PA, Ng D, et al. (2013). Reduced aflatoxin exposure presages decline in liver cancer mortality in an endemic region. Cancer Prevention Research, 6(10), 1038-1045. <https://doi.org/10.1158/1940-6207.CAPR-13-0168>; Liu Y, Wu F (2010). Global burden of aflatoxin-induced hepatocellular carcinoma: a risk assessment. 2-3.title: Don’t rely solely on willpower to quit smoking — get medication first: success rates more than double
2-3.cost: Nicotine patches and gum are over-the-counter products available at any pharmacy. A full course lasts 8–12 weeks and costs several thousand rupees at Indian pharmacy prices; a strip of nine 2 mg nicotine gums costs about ₹75–₹105, and a course takes many strips. Varenicline and bupropion, on the other hand, are prescription-only drugs; you’ll need a prescription from a smoking cessation clinic or a pulmonology department. These costs are roughly offset by the money saved from buying fewer cigarettes during the same period.
2-3.inPlainWords: Relying on sheer willpower alone rarely works for most smokers. People taking varenicline are more than twice as likely to succeed compared to those taking a placebo. Those using nicotine replacement products also have a 50% higher success rate than non-medication users. Combining patches with gum or lozenges further boosts success rates by roughly 20%.
2-3.benefit: A pooled analysis of 41 randomized trials involving 17,395 participants shows that varenicline increases smoking cessation rates by 2.32 times compared to placebo (RR 2.32, 95% CI 2.15–2.51; high-certainty evidence). Varenicline also outperforms bupropion (RR 1.36, a 36% relative increase) and single-form nicotine replacement therapy (RR 1.25, a 25% relative increase). Across 133 trials with 64,640 participants, nicotine replacement products raise success rates by about 55% versus no medication at all (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.49–1.61). Using both a patch and a fast-acting form such as gum or lozenges yields a 27% relative improvement over patch-only use (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37; high-certainty evidence from 16 trials with 12,169 participants).
2-3.sources: Livingstone-Banks J, Fanshawe TR, Thomas KH, et al. (2023). Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 5, CD006103. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD006103.pub8>; Hartmann-Boyce J, Chepkin SC, Ye W, Bullen C, Lancaster T (2018). Nicotine replacement therapy versus control for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 5, CD000146. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000146.pub5>; Theodoulou A, Chepkin SC, Ye W, et al. (2023). Different doses, durations and modes of delivery of nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 6, CD013308. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD013308.pub2>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
2-3.caveats: Common side effects of varenicline include nausea, vivid dreams, and sleep disturbances; anyone with a psychiatric history should discuss this with their doctor. A typical course of nicotine replacement therapy lasts 8–12 weeks — do not abruptly stop use but taper off gradually under medical guidance. While these medications ease withdrawal symptoms during the first few weeks, they do not eliminate cravings triggered by specific situations, so they should be used alongside the other strategies outlined in this chapter: setting a quit date (Section 4) and seeking professional help at a smoking cessation clinic (Section 5).

2-6.title: Only consider e‑cigarettes if you’ve already tried quitting; non‑smokers should avoid them
2-6.cost: In India, no e-cigarette may be produced, imported, sold or stored at all, so there is no lawful price to quote: any device or cartridge you are offered is illicit, and you have no way of checking what is actually in the liquid.
2-6.inPlainWords: Switching to nicotine‑containing e‑cigarettes helps roughly 60% more people quit smoking than nicotine patches — this finding is quite reliable. However, e‑cigarettes are not harmless; long‑term safety data remain limited. For people who have never smoked, there is absolutely no benefit to using them.
2-6.benefit: This up‑to‑date review includes 80 randomized trials involving 29,861 participants. Compared with nicotine replacement therapy, e‑cigarettes raise the quit rate by about 61% (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.23–2.12; high‑certainty evidence based on 11 trials with 4,114 participants). In absolute terms, that translates to roughly 4 extra quitters per 100 users (range: 1–7). The rate of serious adverse events is similar between groups (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.01–0.02; moderate‑certainty evidence). Compared with behavioral support alone or no support at all, e‑cigarettes improve quit rates by about 75% (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.39–2.20; low‑certainty evidence).
2-6.sources: Lindson N, Livingstone-Banks J, Butler AR, et al. (2026). Electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 8, CD010216. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD010216.pub11>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; The Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019. <https://indiankanoon.org/doc/51727498/>
2-6.caveats: This topic is controversial. WHO does not recommend e-cigarettes as a smoking-cessation tool, citing insufficient long-term safety data and concerns that they may attract youth to nicotine. The UK, however, includes them in its quit-smoking services. In India there is no lawful route at all: the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes (Production, Manufacture, Import, Export, Transport, Sale, Distribution, Storage and Advertisement) Act, 2019 prohibits every one of those activities, with a penalty of up to one year’s imprisonment or a ₹1,00,000 fine for a first offence and up to three years or ₹5,00,000 for a repeat. Every device, cartridge or refill liquid you are offered is therefore illicit and unregulated, whatever the packet says. Consequently, fruit-flavored e-cigarettes that are still available are sold through illicit channels outside any regulatory oversight. This is also how synthetic-cannabinoid-laced “high-effect” e-cigarettes enter the market; see Chapter 22, Item 4 (“Do not accept unknown cartridges”). The review examined only legally regulated nicotine-containing products; unverified e-liquid mixtures were not included. As a first step, it is advisable to try the medication described in Item 3 of this section, which offers stronger evidence and lower cost.

2-47.title: Avoid eating raw or drunken freshwater fish and shrimp (including freshwater sashimi, raw fish porridge, and drunken prawns); if you have eaten them regularly, test for liver flukes and take prescribed praziquantel
2-47.cost: Avoiding raw freshwater fish costs nothing; the difficulty is breaking long-standing regional dietary customs and declining dishes during social dinners. If you have eaten freshwater sashimi in the past, a hospital stool microscopy test for fluke eggs costs a few hundred rupees. If infected, physician-prescribed praziquantel is taken over 1 to 2 days.
2-47.inPlainWords: The liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis is an established biological carcinogen: infected people face roughly 4 to 5 times the risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer) compared to uninfected peers. Condiments like vinegar, alcohol, and wasabi do not reliably kill liver fluke larvae. Once diagnosed, a two-day course of prescription anthelmintic medication cures over 90% of infections.
2-47.benefit: Clonorchis sinensis was evaluated in 2009 by the WHO International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and classified as a Group 1 biological carcinogen causing cholangiocarcinoma (upgraded from Group 2A in 1994). A comprehensive meta-analysis of risk factors found that liver fluke infection was associated with a 4.8-fold increase in cholangiocarcinoma risk (relative risk 4.8, 95% CI 2.8–8.4), surpassing the relative risks of hepatitis B (2.6) and hepatitis C (1.8). Another systematic review pooling 36 studies reported odds ratios for cholangiocarcinoma of 4.37 (95% CI 2.84–6.72) in case-control studies and a relative risk of 10.43 (95% CI 2.90–37.47) in cohort studies. Infection was also associated with marked elevations in cholangitis and cholecystitis (RR 7.80), gallstones (RR 2.42), and hepatocellular carcinoma (OR 4.69). Effective destruction requires continuous freezing below -20°C for at least 7 days, or cooking until internal food temperature exceeds 70°C for over 10 minutes. Marinated and cold-smoked freshwater fish also remain infectious. For medical treatment, a 2022 network meta-analysis of 26 trials comprising 3,340 participants demonstrated that the WHO-recommended oral praziquantel regimen (25 mg/kg three times daily for 2 days) achieved an estimated cure rate of 98.5% (95% CI 85.4%–99.9%) against Clonorchis sinensis.
2-47.sources: IARC Working Group on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans (2012). Opisthorchis viverrini and Clonorchis sinensis. In: Biological Agents. IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, Vol. 100B, 341-370. <https://publications.iarc.who.int/119>; Shin HR, Oh JK, Masuyer E, et al. (2010). Epidemiology of cholangiocarcinoma: an update focusing on risk factors. Cancer Science, 101(3), 579-585. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1349-7006.2009.01458.x>; Xia J, Jiang SC, Peng HJ (2015). Association between liver fluke infection and hepatobiliary pathological changes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS ONE, 10(7), e0132673. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0132673>; Qian MB, Patel C, Palmeirim MS, et al. (2022). Efficacy of drugs against clonorchiasis and opisthorchiasis: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. The Lancet Microbe, 3(8), e616-e624. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S2666-5247(22)00026-X>; Centre for Food Safety, Hong Kong. Food Safety of Freshwater Fish Sashimi. <https://www.cfs.gov.hk/sc_chi/multimedia/multimedia_pub/multimedia_pub_fsf_148_01.html>; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Indian Council of Medical Research. <https://www.icmr.gov.in/>
2-47.caveats: Risk estimates derive from observational case-control and prospective registries rather than randomized controlled trials. Cholangiocarcinoma is relatively rare in the absolute population, meaning that despite elevated relative risk, absolute risk remains modest for people outside the regions where raw freshwater fish is everyday food. Grade B is assigned. Adult liver flukes can survive inside the human bile duct system for 20 to 30 years; mild chronic infections often produce zero symptoms, so individuals with regular raw freshwater fish exposure should not wait for symptoms before testing. Stool microscopy for ova provides definitive diagnosis; liver ultrasound, CT, and serology are supportive. Praziquantel dosing must be determined by a physician based on body weight and infection severity; in areas where cysticercosis is co-endemic, detailed medical history is required before high-dose therapy to avoid neurological adverse events. Cured individuals can be reinfected if they continue eating raw freshwater fish. Always use separate knives and chopping boards for raw seafood versus cooked foods. Marine sashimi carries different parasites (such as Anisakis larvae). Pregnant women, young children, and older adults should strictly avoid raw seafood. Hepatitis B and C also induce liver malignancy, detailed in Chapter 1, Item 14, and Chapter 1, Item 45. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and dining companions.

2-13.caveats: The main issues to address are insufficient sleep and irregular schedules; there’s no need to deliberately shorten sleep time. The elevated risk seen in long sleepers is likely reversed causality — depression, chronic illness, and sleep apnea tend to cause longer sleep durations. Currently, only two longitudinal studies support the benefit of a regular schedule; both are observational and ungrouped, so they constitute B‑grade evidence on their own. For ways to recover after staying up late, see Section 38 (recovering sleep after a late night).

2-29.title: Switching from coal and wood to electricity or gas for cooking and heating
2-29.cost: Rural households must replace their stoves and pay higher fuel costs: 8–12 refills of a 14.2 kg cooking-gas cylinder a year come to roughly ₹7,500–₹12,500, at about ₹940–₹1,030 a cylinder. This is a one-time change that doesn’t require ongoing effort. In cities, most households already use electricity or gas.
2-29.inPlainWords: People who cook with coal or wood face roughly a 10% higher chance of dying over the same period compared to those using electricity or gas. For those who heat their homes with coal or wood, the risk is about 14% higher. Those who have already switched to cleaner fuels have a mortality risk that is 13%–33% lower than those still relying on coal or wood.
2-29.benefit: In a prospective cohort of 271,217 adults in five rural areas, followed for a mean of 7.2 years, individuals who cooked using solid fuels such as coal or wood had a mortality risk roughly 11% higher (HR 1.11) than those using electricity or gas. Those who used solid fuels for heating faced a 14% higher risk (HR 1.14). Among people who had switched from solid fuels to cleaner alternatives, the risk dropped by 13% for cooking (HR 0.87) and by 33% for heating (HR 0.67). Separate data also show that for every 10 µg/m³ increase in long-term exposure to outdoor PM2.5, the risk of death from natural causes rises by roughly 8% (RR 1.08). Natural causes refer to deaths not resulting from accidents.
2-29.sources: Yu K, Qiu G, Chan KH, et al. (2018). JAMA, 319(13), 1351-1361. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.2151> (the published title names the country of the cohort, so it is omitted here; the DOI resolves to the full record); Chen J, Hoek G (2020). Long-term exposure to PM and all-cause and cause-specific mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Environment International. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2020.105974>
2-29.caveats: These studies merely track health outcomes over time. Households that switch to cleaner fuels are often wealthier, so part of the observed 0.67-fold reduction in risk is likely linked to socioeconomic factors. Regarding outdoor PM2.5, individual actions such as relocating, wearing masks, or using air purifiers have limited impact. There are no studies evaluating air purifiers based on mortality rates, so no specific figures are provided here.

2-39.caveats: All these findings come from observational studies without subgroup adjustments. Night-shift workers naturally differ from others in smoking habits, weight, and income, and full adjustments are hard to achieve. Cancer risk evidence is weaker than popular claims suggest. A pooled analysis of 12 studies involving 12,132 breast cancer cases found only a 5% higher risk among night-shift workers (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.96–1.14). Therefore, this analysis focuses on cardiovascular risk, not cancer. Not everyone must leave night shifts; you should weigh the long-term costs yourself. For those already working nights, several steps help: quit smoking (see Section 1); control blood pressure and cholesterol per medical advice (Section 12); and make up lost sleep after shifts (Section 38). Two additional strategies are worth trying: eat mainly during daylight hours, and use bright light during shifts plus near-total darkness during daytime rest to reset your circadian rhythm. Only the latter has proven effective at shifting the rhythm; ordinary indoor lighting leaves it unchanged even after six night shifts. Bright light at 7,000–12,000 lux combined with near-total darkness restores it in four days. Crucially, all three measures — bright night-time light, strict daytime darkness, and sunglasses on the way home — must be used together; skipping any one negates the effect. Both strategies affect metabolism and sleep only; no trials have shown they lower cardiovascular risk. On days off, returning to a daytime routine resets the rhythm again. Full numbers and sources are set out in the research notes for this chapter.

2-12.title: Screen blood lipids regularly in adulthood (every 2 to 5 years before age 40, annually from age 40); take prescribed medication consistently for hypertension and dyslipidemia, never stopping on your own
2-12.cost: Generic hypertension drugs and statins cost a few hundred rupees a month at a private pharmacy and considerably less at a government hospital. They are taken once daily, requiring minimal time. The real challenge is sticking to them long-term rather than stopping once you feel better. Checking blood lipids requires a blood draw. The free public route is the health and wellness centre, where adults from age 30 are screened for high blood pressure, diabetes and the three common cancers; India has no nationwide free annual check-up for people over 65, so a lipid test is either paid for or done on a doctor’s order.
2-12.inPlainWords: For every 10 mmHg drop in systolic blood pressure, mortality decreases by roughly 13%, while stroke risk drops by about 27%. Each 1.0 mmol/L reduction in LDL cholesterol achieved by statins lowers mortality by roughly 10%. Those who take their medication as directed have a 30% to 45% lower risk of death compared to those who frequently miss doses. Adults should check blood lipids every 2 to 5 years before age 40, and annually starting at age 40.
2-12.benefit: Pooled data from multiple randomized controlled trials show that a 10 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure lowers mortality by about 13% (RR 0.87) and major cardiovascular events by roughly 20% (RR 0.80). Stroke risk drops by around 27% (RR 0.73), while heart failure risk decreases by about 28% (RR 0.72). Statins also reduce LDL cholesterol; each 1.0 mmol/L drop lowers mortality by roughly 10% (RR 0.90) and major vascular events by about 22% (RR 0.78). Observational studies further indicate that patients who adhere to prescribed treatment regimens (at least 80% compliance) enjoy significantly lower mortality rates: statin adherence reduces risk by about 45% (RR 0.55), while adherence to antihypertensive therapy lowers risk by roughly 29% (RR 0.71).
2-12.sources: Ettehad D et al. (2016). Blood pressure lowering for prevention of cardiovascular disease and death: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Lancet. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(15)01225-8>; Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' (CTT) Collaboration (2010). Efficacy and safety of more intensive lowering of LDL cholesterol: a meta-analysis of data from 170 000 participants in 26 randomised trials. Lancet. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61350-5>; Chowdhury R et al. (2013). Adherence to cardiovascular therapy: a meta-analysis of prevalence and clinical consequences. European Heart Journal. <https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/eht295>
2-12.caveats: Only individuals deemed by doctors to need medication should follow this advice; healthy people do not require medication. The figures regarding consistent medication use stem from observational data; those who stick to treatment tend to be more disciplined overall, which may inflate perceived benefits. The mortality reductions linked to blood pressure control and statins are firmly supported by randomized trials. Routine lipid screening catches silent hyperlipidemia early before coronary artery disease or stroke occurs. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and your parents.

2-42.title: Turn on the range hood while stir-frying and deep-frying, from the moment you light the stove until the cooking is done.
2-42.cost: For households already equipped with a range hood, the extra expense is just a bit more on the electricity bill. For those without one, buying and installing a unit costs roughly ₹5,000–₹25,000, and a chimney that vents outside costs more than a recirculating model. The real challenge is remembering to turn it on every time you cook — don’t turn it off just because it makes noise.
2-42.inPlainWords: Among non-smoking women, those who do most of the cooking at home and rarely or never use a range hood face roughly twice the risk of developing lung cancer compared with those who use one regularly. Living in a kitchen with poor ventilation also raises this risk by about 50%, with the effect being most pronounced among households that burn coal.
2-42.benefit: Thirteen case-control studies among non-smoking women were pooled for analysis. In these studies, researchers compared lung cancer patients with healthy individuals, asking about past cooking habits. Overall, exposure to cooking fumes was linked to a 1.74-fold increase in lung cancer risk (95% CI 1.57–1.94). Four of these studies specifically looked at women who used no range hood while cooking; their risk was 2.11 times higher (95% CI 1.54–2.89). One Taiwanese study compared 1,302 non-smoking women with lung cancer to 1,302 healthy women, focusing on those with at least ten years of cooking experience. Women who used their range hood for more than two-thirds of those years had roughly half the risk of developing lung cancer compared to those who used it for less than a third of the time (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32–0.76). A Shanghai-based prospective study followed 71,000 non-smoking women from 1996 to 2009, identifying 429 cases of lung cancer. Women who reported living in a poorly ventilated kitchen had a 49% higher risk of lung cancer (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.15–1.95). Those who had burned coal in such kitchens for over 20 years faced a 2.03-fold increase in risk (HR 2.03, 95% CI 1.35–3.05). No significant difference in risk was found between women who did and did not burn coal at all (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.84–1.26), nor between those using different types of cooking oil.
2-42.sources: Xue Y, Jiang Y, Jin S, Li Y (2016). OncoTargets and Therapy, 9, 2987-2992. <https://doi.org/10.2147/OTT.S100949>; Chen TY, et al. (2020). Scientific Reports, 10(1), 6774. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-63656-7>; Kim C, Gao YT, Xiang YB, et al. (2015). International Journal of Cancer, 136(3), 632-638. <https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.29020>; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>. The published titles of the three studies name the country or city the study populations came from and are omitted here; each DOI resolves to the full record.
2-42.caveats: There is some debate regarding these findings: the evidence supporting regular range hood use comes largely from case-control studies done in Shanghai and in Taiwan, and no Indian study has measured the effect here. Since participants recall past habits after being diagnosed with lung cancer, they may underreport how often they used their range hoods, potentially inflating the observed risk figures. The Shanghai study showed the greatest risk increase among households burning coal in poorly ventilated kitchens; it did not provide separate risk estimates for households using only gas. For this reason, the overall evidence grade is set at B, while the benefit is considered substantial based on the roughly twofold difference in risk. Women who regularly do the cooking at home are the primary beneficiaries of this measure; see Item 29 of this chapter for more information on avoiding coal and wood for cooking and heating.

2-25.title: Drinking tea more than three times a week
2-25.cost: Brewing at home costs a few hundred rupees a year — a 1 kg pack of leaf tea costs about ₹500 and lasts a year or more at three or more cups a week — and a cup at a tea stall costs about ₹10–₹20. Brewing a cup takes only a few minutes, so it doesn’t take up much time at all.
2-25.inPlainWords: People who regularly drink tea have a roughly 15% lower chance of dying during the same period. Starting at age 50, they can expect to live 1.26 years longer on average, and 1.41 extra years without developing any cardiovascular diseases.
2-25.benefit: In a prospective cohort of 100,902 adults followed for a median of 7.3 years, people with a regular tea-drinking habit had a 15% lower risk of death (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.79–0.90, which is a reliable range). For those starting at age 50, regular tea drinkers gain 1.41 extra years free from atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases, and 1.26 extra years of overall life expectancy.
2-25.sources: Wang X, Liu F, Li J, et al. (2020). European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 27(18), 1956-1963. <https://doi.org/10.1177/2047487319894685>; Cui P, Li Y, Yan S, et al. (2020). Food and Chemical Toxicology, 146, 111830. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fct.2020.111830>; Zhou H, Yan S, Yao X, et al. (2022). Toxins, 14(7), 452. <https://doi.org/10.3390/toxins14070452>; Hu J, Webster D, Cao J, Shao A (2018). Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yrtph.2018.03.019>. The published titles of the first three papers name the country or city the study population came from, so the titles are omitted here; each DOI resolves to the full record.
2-25.caveats: Tea drinkers in this cohort were also more likely than non-drinkers to smoke and to drink alcohol, and the researchers adjusted for these and other factors, but not all. Also, avoid drinking tea that is excessively hot; refer to the section on hot drink temperatures for more details. Some people worry about mycotoxins in tea; tests on 158 batches of dark tea found aflatoxin in just 2 batches, and the amount consumed via normal tea intake stays well below internationally accepted limits. Another study examining 352 tea samples for 16 types of mycotoxins found that only ochratoxin A in dark tea exceeded the safety limit on average, but even this amount is not considered a dietary risk for regular tea drinkers. Keep tea stored in a dry place, and discard any batches that have become damp or moldy. Tea extract capsules are a different story: taking large doses of concentrated catechins at one time can damage the liver, but this risk does not apply to brewed tea at all. Therefore, all the benefits mentioned here apply only to brewed tea, not to any tea extract supplements.

2-34.cost: About ₹30–₹70 a day for 300–500 ml of milk or curd, depending on whether you buy packet milk, loose milk or curd from a dairy, with no extra time required.

2-9.title: Switch household salt to low‑sodium (potassium‑rich) salt
2-9.cost: A 1 kg bag costs roughly ₹20–₹30 more than regular salt. It’s easy to switch when you shop, adding virtually no extra time. The taste stays almost the same.
2-9.inPlainWords: For people who have had a stroke or are over 60 with hypertension, switching to low‑sodium salt can lower their chance of dying within five years by about 12% and the risk of another stroke by roughly 14%.
2-9.benefit: In a trial of 20,995 people across 600 villages, half were given a salt substitute (about three-quarters sodium chloride and one-quarter potassium chloride) instead of ordinary salt and were followed for about five years. Those using low‑sodium salt had a 12% lower risk of death (RR 0.88), a 14% lower risk of stroke (RR 0.86), and a 13% lower risk of major cardiovascular events (RR 0.87) compared with the regular‑salt group. No statistically significant difference emerged between the groups regarding episodes of excessively high blood potassium levels.
2-9.sources: Neal B et al. (2021). Effect of Salt Substitution on Cardiovascular Events and Death. NEJM. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2105675>; O'Donnell M et al. (2014). Urinary sodium and potassium excretion, mortality, and cardiovascular events. NEJM. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1311889> (disputing party PURE)
2-9.caveats: This finding is somewhat controversial. The PURE study only recorded long‑term outcomes without random assignment; it reported that individuals excreting less than 3 g of sodium per day faced a roughly 27% higher risk of death or cardiovascular events, while those excreting more than 7 g per day faced a 15% higher risk. According to PURE, both very low and very high sodium intake are detrimental, with moderate intake being optimal. Moreover, the trial involved only high‑risk elderly participants; younger, healthier individuals would likely gain far less benefit. People with impaired kidney function or those taking potassium‑sparing medications should consult a physician before making this switch.

2-10.cost: Dental floss or interdental brushes cost a few hundred rupees a year — a 50 m floss pack costs about ₹125 — while professional cleanings run about ₹800–₹2,500 each at a private clinic, depending on the city. It takes only two to three extra minutes per day. The real challenge is making flossing a daily habit.

2-22.cost: Consuming 28 grams per day costs roughly ₹8,000–₹12,000 annually at Indian retail prices for almonds; peanuts cost a fraction of that, and cashews and pistachios cost more. It’s easy to fit into your routine without taking extra time.

2-26.cost: Making coffee at home costs roughly ₹15–₹35 a day for three to four cups: a 100 g jar of instant coffee costs about ₹350–₹400 and lasts about a fortnight at that rate. It takes only a few minutes to brew a cup, so it doesn’t take up much time at all.

2-27.cost: It costs roughly ₹30–₹60 a day for 400 g of seasonal fruit and vegetables. You also need to spend some time washing and chopping them. The real challenge is buying and eating the required amount every single day.

2-45.title: If diagnosed with prediabetes (elevated blood glucose below diabetes threshold), delay progression through dietary caloric restriction, weight loss, and increased physical activity; retest glucose every six months
2-45.cost: Zero financial cost; eating less saves a little money. Accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity (such as brisk walking) per week, averaging ~20 minutes daily. Reduce daily caloric intake by 400 to 500 kcal compared to baseline. The primary difficulty is lifelong consistency and preventing weight regain once lost. Retest blood glucose every six months (fasting blood glucose costs about ₹80–₹200 at a private lab, less at a government hospital).
2-45.inPlainWords: For individuals with elevated blood glucose who have not yet reached the diagnostic threshold for diabetes, eating less, moving more, and losing a modest amount of weight reduces the risk of progressing to full diabetes by 30% to 60%. However, similar trials in the US and Finland did not observe statistically significant differences in all-cause mortality.
2-45.benefit: The Da Qing Diabetes Prevention Study was a clinic-randomized trial conducted in Da Qing, Heilongjiang Province, enrolling 577 adults with impaired glucose tolerance (a form of prediabetes) assigned to control or three 6-year intervention arms: diet alone, exercise alone, or combined diet plus exercise. Six-year cumulative diabetes incidence was 67.7% in controls versus 43.8% (diet), 41.1% (exercise), and 46.0% (combined). After adjusting for baseline BMI and fasting glucose, diabetes risk fell by 31%, 46%, and 42% respectively, with comparable reductions across lean and overweight subgroups (BMI cutoff 25). At 23-year follow-up, the combined intervention group had 41% lower cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.36–0.96), 29% lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.51–0.99), and 45% lower diabetes incidence (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.40–0.76). At 30-year follow-up, median onset of diabetes was delayed by 3.96 years; composite cardiovascular events were 26% lower (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.59–0.92), severe microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) were 35% lower (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.45–0.95), cardiovascular mortality was 33% lower (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48–0.94), all-cause mortality was 26% lower (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61–0.89), and mean survival was prolonged by 1.44 years (95% CI 0.20–2.68). In the U.S. Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) trial of 3,234 adults with prediabetes, the intensive lifestyle arm targeted at least 7% weight loss and at least 150 minutes a week physical activity: over a mean 2.8-year period, diabetes incidence fell by 58% (95% CI 48%–66%) compared to placebo, while metformin reduced incidence by 31% (95% CI 17%–43%). Over 15-year follow-up, lifestyle intervention maintained a 27% diabetes reduction (HR 0.73), though between-group divergence narrowed. At 21-year median follow-up, all-cause mortality (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.81–1.28) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.77–1.81) showed no significant differences compared to controls. In the Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study (DPS) of 522 overweight adults with impaired glucose tolerance, lifestyle intervention reduced 4-year cumulative diabetes incidence by 58% (11% vs 23%), maintaining a 43% reduction at median 7-year follow-up; at 10.6 years, all-cause mortality showed no significant difference (HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.21–1.58).
2-45.sources: Pan XR, Li GW, Hu YH, et al. (1997). Effects of diet and exercise in preventing NIDDM in people with impaired glucose tolerance. The Da Qing IGT and Diabetes Study. Diabetes Care, 20(4), 537-544. <https://doi.org/10.2337/diacare.20.4.537>; Li G, Zhang P, Wang J, et al. (2014). Cardiovascular mortality, all-cause mortality, and diabetes incidence after lifestyle intervention for people with impaired glucose tolerance in the Da Qing Diabetes Prevention Study: a 23-year follow-up study. Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, 2(6), 474-480. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(14)70057-9>; Gong Q, Zhang P, Wang J, et al. (2019). Morbidity and mortality after lifestyle intervention for people with impaired glucose tolerance: 30-year results of the Da Qing Diabetes Prevention Outcome Study. Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, 7(6), 452-461. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(19)30093-2>; Knowler WC, Barrett-Connor E, Fowler SE, et al. (2002). Reduction in the incidence of type 2 diabetes with lifestyle intervention or metformin. NEJM, 346(6), 393-403. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa012512>; Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group (2015). Long-term effects of lifestyle intervention or metformin on diabetes development and microvascular complications over 15-year follow-up: the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study. Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, 3(11), 866-875. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(15)00291-0>; Lee CG, Heckman-Stoddard B, Dabelea D, et al. (2021). Effect of Metformin and Lifestyle Interventions on Mortality in the Diabetes Prevention Program and Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study. Diabetes Care, 44(12), 2775-2782. <https://doi.org/10.2337/dc21-1046>; Tuomilehto J, Lindström J, Eriksson JG, et al. (2001). Prevention of type 2 diabetes mellitus by changes in lifestyle among subjects with impaired glucose tolerance. NEJM, 344(18), 1343-1350. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200105033441801>; Lindström J, Ilanne-Parikka P, Peltonen M, et al. (2006). Sustained reduction in the incidence of type 2 diabetes by lifestyle intervention: follow-up of the Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study. Lancet, 368(9548), 1673-1679. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(06)69701-8>; Uusitupa M, Peltonen M, Lindström J, et al. (2009). Ten-year mortality and cardiovascular morbidity in the Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study—secondary analysis of the randomized trial. PLoS ONE, 4(5), e5656. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0005656>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>
2-45.caveats: Controverted regarding mortality endpoints. All three major trials conclusively demonstrate reduced and delayed diabetes incidence; however, a statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality was observed only in the Da Qing trial (which enrolled 577 participants, originally powered for diabetes incidence rather than mortality). In the U.S. DPP, once the randomized phase concluded, all arms including placebo were offered group lifestyle classes. In the Finnish DPS, statistical power for subtle mortality differences was limited. Therefore, delaying diabetes progression is firmly proven, while mortality extension remains an open question. Participants in the U.S. and Finnish trials had baseline BMI >30, whereas Da Qing participants averaged BMI 25.7, with notable benefits even in participants with minimal weight loss, suggesting dietary composition and physical movement drive benefits independently of mass reduction alone. Start by eliminating sugary drinks (Chapter 2, Item 7). Activity targets are detailed in Chapter 2, Item 11 (7,000–8,000 steps daily). BMI targets are outlined in Chapter 2, Item 32 (BMI 20–25). Screening thresholds are described in Chapter 1, Item 8 (fasting blood glucose screening). Metformin also delays diabetes onset but is less effective than lifestyle modification; its initiation requires medical prescription. Benefit magnitude is categorized as High based on the 26% reduction in all-cause mortality in the Da Qing trial. Primary beneficiary is yourself.

2-20.title: People who drink daily and experience tremors and palpitations when they stop should not try to quit on their own
2-20.cost: Seeing a psychiatrist or addiction specialist costs about ₹500–₹1,500 for a private consultation, and far less at a government hospital. In severe cases, a short hospital stay may be required.
2-20.inPlainWords: Individuals who consume large amounts of alcohol every day can suffer from withdrawal symptoms when they suddenly stop. Mild cases involve tremors, sweating, palpitations, and insomnia; severe cases may lead to seizures or delirium tremens — a life‑threatening emergency. A nationwide Norwegian health registry follow-up found that those who had experienced delirium tremens had an 8% annual mortality rate thereafter. If you wish to quit, consult a doctor first and describe exactly how much you drink each day.
2-20.benefit: A 2026 clinical review notes that chronic heavy drinkers often develop withdrawal syndrome after abrupt cessation or a major reduction in intake; symptoms include tremors, autonomic hyperactivity, anxiety, insomnia, perceptual disturbances, seizures, and delirium tremens — conditions that are “common and potentially fatal” in general medical practice. Norway’s nationwide registry included 36,287 individuals diagnosed with alcohol dependence, withdrawal states, or delirium tremens between 2009 and 2015. The annual mortality rate was 8.0% in the delirium tremens group, 5.0% in the withdrawal state group, and 3.6% in the alcohol dependence group. The standardized mortality ratio for the delirium tremens group was 9.8 (95% CI 8.9–10.7), indicating that their risk of death is roughly 9.8 times higher than that of age‑matched peers.
2-20.sources: Caputo F, Lungaro L, Costanzini A, De Giorgio R, Addolorato G (2026). Alcohol withdrawal syndrome in hospitalized patients: a practical review. European Journal of Internal Medicine, 107103. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejim.2026.107103>; Bramness JG, Heiberg IH, Høye A, Rossow I (2023). Mortality and alcohol-related morbidity in patients with delirium tremens, alcohol withdrawal state or alcohol dependence in Norway: A register-based prospective cohort study. Addiction, 118(12), 2352–2359. <https://doi.org/10.1111/add.16297>
2-20.caveats: How to tell if you need help: If you drink almost every day, experience tremors, sweating, palpitations, or insomnia when you skip a day, or feel better after a morning drink, you should not attempt to quit on your own. Standard medical treatment involves using benzodiazepines to manage the acute phase and administering thiamine (vitamin B1) supplementation. The B grade reflects that the Norwegian data describe “what happens to people who have already had delirium tremens” rather than “what occurs when someone tries to quit independently”; the link between these two situations is an inference. Quitting alcohol is still advisable, but it should be done under medical supervision. For guidance on moderate drinking levels, see section 19; strategies for reducing intake are outlined in section 21.
